description: I am the master of all Trades.
summary:
EmberLens is a satellite fire intelligence platform. It handles a pretty specific problem. It lines up NASA fire data from different sensors despite clashing resolutions.

With seven million records, it lets you map fires, match sensors, and check seasons. The backend runs on Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and basic web tools.

A big use case is tracking crop burning across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi NCR. Down the line, the team wants to pull in ISRO satellite feeds, weather data, and risk forecasting.

The goal is pretty simple. It cleans up messy satellite feeds so researchers skip sensor quirks entirely.
details:
EmberLens is a web-based satellite fire intelligence platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 by Team Master of All Trades. It looks at and compares fire detections from NASA sensors, specifically MODIS and VIIRS. Since these satellites use different resolutions, a one-kilometer sensor compared directly to a 375-meter sensor can give you misleading numbers.

We pulled in over 7.43 million records from NASA FIRMS. You get live fire maps, past coverage stats, and seasonal trends right away. It uses geographic grids and basic stats to make the different satellite observations actually comparable.

The main benefit is that it takes complicated satellite data and makes it easier to understand. No tech background is needed to figure out this dashboard. Researchers can review fire history, check sensor data, and spot odd seasons without digging through raw tables.

We want to improve environmental monitoring and help data-driven research. One real use case is studying agricultural residue burning in places like Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi NCR, where seasonal fires cause heavy air pollution. Down the road, we want to add Indian satellites, weather data, and AI fire-risk forecasting.

We built the app using Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SQL. The backend runs on FastAPI and Uvicorn, backed by an SQLite database storing millions of records. We also pulled in data from the Microsoft Planetary Computer and Meteomatics for extra environmental context. It runs on ordinary hardware so you do not need any expensive gear.

Most fire maps just show you dots on a screen. EmberLens tries to figure out why different satellites report different fire counts in the first place. We combine sensor-aware statistical harmonization with seasonal analysis and interactive visuals. One thing we cared about was scientific transparency. Missing numbers get handled properly instead of being marked as zero fires. That prevents misleading conclusions when you are looking at historical gaps.

We balanced accuracy, speed, and usability while keeping costs low and the science solid. The setup handles fresh satellite feeds while keeping past trends separate from future guesses.

At the end of the day, EmberLens helps turn messy satellite observations into clearer fire intelligence. Different Satellites. One Clearer Picture.
